This page sets out the whole exercise. The [case study](index.qmd) presents the original study, the Multi100 project and the five reanalyses in full, and it is the place to start if you have not read it. Your work happens in the workspace you downloaded and opened in your IDE; the [Browser lab](lab.qmd) runs the same exercise in a browser tab, for following a demonstration, for trying it without an installation, and as a fallback. Come back here whenever you want the overview again.

---

## The claim you are working on

Five independent analysts reanalysed a claim made by the original author (OA) as part of the Multi100 project. The claim, as presented to all analysts, was:

> "…poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016, p. 619)

The published coefficient – the specific number that the Task 2 constraints pointed to – is:

> **Unemployment → cosmopolitan EU framing: b = −0.0034, t = −4.03, p < .001** (Table 3, Model 1)

This comes from a three-level random-intercept model using pooled Eurobarometer data (16 waves, 2004–2013, 27 EU countries). Your first job is to reproduce, on the country-year panel, the result that analyst C6HJR recorded for this claim (t = −3.804, in Task 3), using a transparent, reproducible pipeline. Your second job is to deviate from it – deliberately, with a written justification – and see what that does to the estimate.

---

## Which claim, and why {#which-claim}

The claim on the card is one of several that the paper makes. The SCORE programme selected claims from published abstracts, and the sentence it took from this paper is the first half of a two-part hypothesis. In the paper itself, that hypothesis reads: "Poor national economic performances significantly increase the negative and decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. The effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions of EU framing" (p. 621). The second sentence, which compares two of the four framing scales with the other two, was not part of the claim given to the analysts, and neither was the second hypothesis of the paper, about the gap between high- and low-educated citizens, which the [individual-level module](../../companion/individual-level.qmd#sec-claim2) takes up. The Multi100 project then narrowed the card further in its constrained phase, fixing the cosmopolitan scale as the outcome and the unemployment rate as the predictor, which is why the coefficient above is the one with which the five results were to be compared.

Each of those steps was a decision that someone other than you made, and each one shaped what "replicating the claim" could mean. Testing the first sentence needs one outcome and one predictor. Testing the second needs a grouping of the scales, and the [measurement module](../../companion/measurement.qmd#sec-theory) shows that the data only half support that grouping. The education hypothesis needs the respondents rather than the country-years. Choosing which sentence to replicate is the first specification decision of any replication, and it is made before the estimand, the graph or the menu, usually by the people who wrote the card. The course keeps to the card, so that its results can be set beside those of the five analysts.

## The five Multi100 analysts {#the-five-published-analysts}

Before you begin, here is what the five Multi100 analysts found when they reanalysed the same claim, as Multi100 recorded it:

| Analyst | Tool | Statistic | N | Partial r, recorded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 018OL | R | t = −1.21 | 420 | −0.060 |
| **C6HJR** | **R** | **t = −3.80** | **270** | **−0.242** |
| KEVF1 | R | t = −5.90 | 209,826 | −0.452 |
| KQXUE | Stata | t = −7.17 | 270 | −0.419 |
| PRL47 | Stata | z = −3.59 | 394,575 | −0.006 |

All five reported a negative effect, in the direction of the original. The recorded partial correlations range from −0.006 to −0.452, a factor of nearly 80, but most of that spread comes from the conversion of each test statistic into a correlation rather than from the analyses themselves. PRL47 and C6HJR report almost the same statistic, yet the z of PRL47 was converted on the number of respondents, which pulls any correlation towards zero. Section 4 of the [case study](index.qmd#sec-recorded) shows how the conversion works, and the [Multiverse page](multiverse.qmd#reference-marks) places each result on the degrees of freedom of its own inference.

---

## The tasks

The exercise runs as five numbered tasks across four 90-minute parts. Each task says what to do in the workspace and, where it differs, on the browser lab page, which produces the same numbers.

### Part 1 – Credibility and tools

**Task 1 – Get yourself running (~8 minutes, and the break if you need it).** The only aim is to reach the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you. There is no prize for finishing early, and getting this right now saves an hour of misery later. *Workspace:* open the workspace folder in your IDE, let the packages install, and render the report skeleton once. If it renders, everything works, and if it does not, `source("R/check_setup.R")` reports what is missing. *Browser lab:* wait for the engine to finish downloading, then run the setup-check cell and confirm the panel has 270 rows. The vocabulary warm-up on the same page – three Rs and one impostor – is there to fill the waiting.

If your installation will not cooperate, do not fight it. Open the browser lab and carry on there; nothing in the day depends on it.

---

### Part 2 – The claim and its estimand

**Task 2 – Meet the panel, name the estimand, draw the graph (~18 minutes).** The task has three parts, taken in order. First, look at the data. The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise – 270 country-years, unemployment and GDP growth alongside several EU-framing measures – and it is published in the main folder of the analyst's OSF fork (`osf.io/6zqct`), while the official Multi100 archival record is at `osf.io/8rtwe`. Run the small-multiples figure and find the countries that move sharply around 2009, because the model uses that within-country variation.

Second, write the **estimand** in words: the unit-specific quantity, the target population, the aggregation. The template gives you the structure, and filling it in makes you say precisely what this claim is about.

Third, complete the **causal graph**. Take the `#` off the arrows you are willing to defend, re-run `adjustmentSets()`, and check which adjustment set the graph now implies. Then two sentences for your notes: what do two-way fixed effects adjust for, and what can they not fix? *Workspace:* edit `R/dag_starter.R`, where every arrow is an ordinary R formula and adopting one means deleting a `#`. *Browser lab:* the same graph, built with `dagify()`. There `adjustmentSets()` prints the answer that dagitty gives for each combination of the arrows in the cell, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty, and the workspace answers for any other graph. The [causal-graphs companion module](../../companion/dags.qmd) works the material through slowly if you want it.

---

### Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration

**Task 3 – Reproduce the recorded result (~22 minutes).** Fit the two-way fixed-effects model that analyst C6HJR chose – `mcosmo ~ unemp_c`, with country and year fixed effects – and confirm you get **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270). This is the reproduction step, and reaching −3.804, the value recorded for analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset, shows that the same data and the same code give the same number. *Workspace:* run the model in your working script. *Browser lab:* fill the gaps in the exercise cell; there are two hints and a full solution, and using them is not cheating.

Your reproduction is one check among several. The paper was also put through attempts at reproduction and replication in the SCORE programme, which section 2 of the [case study](index.qmd#sec-repetition) describes.

**Task 4 – Work the menu (~20 minutes).** This task is **exploratory**. Try several specifications from the [specification menu](menu.qmd), see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. `try_spec()` takes one argument per decision and every argument defaults to the specification that you just reproduced, so changing one thing means changing one argument. An option that is not on the curve, such as pooled OLS (`estimator = "pooled_cl"`), stops with the reason that it left the curve and the page of the course that teaches it. `my_experiments()` prints everything you have tried, side by side – the small multiverse you have just built. Then pick the one you would defend if you had to, and `submit_exploration()` puts it on the live [Multiverse](multiverse.qmd) chart as an **exploratory** result, drawn in green.

Nothing in this task is preregistered. You are allowed to look, change your mind and try again, and the chart labels the result as exploratory for that reason.

---

### Part 4 – Multiverse and preregistration

Part 4 opens with a reading of the class results: the class chart laid over the curve of 864 specifications, which decisions move the result most, where the five reanalyses and the original study sit on the main chart, and **your own placement**, the share of the 864 specifications that lie further in the direction of the claim than the estimate you submitted. It then turns to what a curve can and cannot establish, and to the argument that once a question is fully specified there is only one correct analysis. The [reading on the specification curve](reading-inference.qmd) is the companion for this part.

**Task 5 – Declare one specification, run it, report it (~20 minutes).** Pick ONE specification from the curve, one option for each of the fourteen decisions on the menu, and complete the preregistration block **before you run that specification**. It is a shortened but real preregistration template: what you are testing, what you already know about the data, your one specification, why those controls (grounded in your Task 2 graph), and the rule you will judge the result by. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the convention for the day and is applied for you. The claim expects framing to rise with growth, so the sign of a growth slope is flipped, and 'supports the claim' then reads as a negative sign for every specification.

Run `prereg()` once that block is complete and before you write the model code below it; the rendered report, which carries the date on which it was rendered, keeps the declaration above the cells that fit the specification. On the browser lab page, copy the block into your notes instead. Then translate the declaration into model syntax yourself – `build_model()` accepts only code that matches what you declared – run it, and `report_result()` prints a one-click, pre-filled form link. Your submission appears on the chart as a **declared** result, drawn in black beside the green exploratory ones.

Task 4 and Task 5 run identical code. What separates them is that an exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit twice so that the two sets of results can be compared side by side.

---

## What counts as a result {#what-makes-a-result-valid}

Your result is valid for the multiverse chart if it:

- is one of the 864 specifications on the curve, so that it reports the coefficient on the predictor that measures economic performance (unemployment or GDP growth, in one of its published series and forms) from a model of the country-year panel,
- is submitted to the class-results form via the `report_result()` link (so that it appears on the live [Multiverse](multiverse.qmd) chart), and
- has a written justification for the choice you made (2 sentences is enough).

The whole exercise depends on the justification. Auspurg & Brüderl (2021) argue that a multiverse of unjustified specifications shows dispersion and nothing more; the stated reasons are what let it count as evidence.
